newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea creditors set Dainong bail-out at $17.8 mln.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea creditors set Dainong bail-out at $17.8 mln.

text.p: South Korean creditor banks decided on Wednesday to extend $17.8 million in emergency loans to help bail out the nation's leading textile and retailing business group, an official at major creditor SEOULBANK said.

Creditors will grant 5.7 billion won ($6.39 million) in rescue loans to major affiliates Dainong Corp and 10.2 billion won to Midopa Department Store on the condition that group family members give control over their shares to creditors.
However, it was not clear whether the family members would agree to give up their rights.
"I believe the management right should belong to the company in order to implement the self-rescue plan and revive the company," group chairman Park Young-il told reporters.
"We'll discuss further this issue with creditors," he said.
Dainong is the second group to be offered a bail-out by a voluntary banking group set up to keep troubled firms afloat.
The 19th-ranked Jinro Group was the first to benefit, with six units tapped for bail-out. But Jinro has received no money yet as its owners have refused to cede control to creditors.
Shares of Dainong Corp and Midopa went to their daily limit high on hopes for the emergency loan from banks. The bank decision was announced after the market closed.
Earlier, a SEOULBANK official said the two companies had requested 78 billion won in total. But a Dainong statement later said they had requested 86.2 billion won.
Separately, the group said it would raise 820 billion won by the end of the first half of 1998 by selling affiliates and real estate to overcome its financial crisis.
A Dainong group statement said it would sell 17 of its 21 affiliates and focus on the remaining four units, Dainong Corp, Midopa, Dainong Heavy Industry Co Ltd and Metro Products Inc.
"We have prepared self-rescue plans to revive the group and have started to put them into practice," said Park Sang-chul, the group's managing director.
As part of its self-rescue plan, Dainong said it would induce capital investment at home and abroad, and switch short-term loans to longer-term, the statement said.
Dainong's debt totalled 1.7 trillion won on 1.5 trillion group turnover last year.
The group spent 128.8 billion won to ward off a hostile takeover bid by Shindongbang Corp early this year. Dainong has said that defence led to its troubles.

"The financial structure of the group weakened following excessive spending to fend off a hostile takeover on Midopa and tighter credit control by banks after the collapse of Hanbo," said director Park.
Analysts said the bail-out would keep the group afloat.
"Its self-rescue plan to restructure its business will be painful but the company is heading in the right direction," said Lee Keun-mo, head of research at ING-Baring Securities.
However, some analysts said the group would face difficulties selling off its affiliates and real estate.

"At a time when most companies are having trouble raising funds, why would anyone go out of their way to buy Dainong's financially troubled affiliates and real estate," said a research head at a local brokerage house who declined to be identified.
"It would be hard to sell all those companies and lands in such a short time."
South Korea has been rocked by a series of corporate failures since early this year. Most recently, the country's leading confectionery maker Samlip General Foods Co filed for receivership.
